body.heading: Lifts that nobody trusted
paragraphs: Hoists existed for centuries — platforms raised by ropes, animals or steam. Factories used them for freight, but people sensibly refused to ride: if the rope broke, the platform fell, and everyone knew it. Buildings stayed low partly because legs, not lifts, set the limit.

In 1852, the mechanic Elisha Otis was asked to build a freight hoist for a factory in New York, and he added a simple guardian: a spring above the platform, held bent by the rope's tension. If the rope went slack, the spring would snap outward and drive toothed bars into the guide rails, locking the platform in place.

body.heading: The demonstration
paragraphs: At the Crystal Palace exhibition in New York in 1854, Otis staged one of the great product demonstrations. Standing on his platform as it rose high above the crowd, he ordered the rope cut. The platform dropped a few centimetres — and stopped. 'All safe, gentlemen, all safe,' he announced, bowing.

Orders followed. In 1857 his company installed a passenger elevator in a New York department store, and the idea of riding a lift stopped seeming reckless. Combined with steel-frame construction later in the century, the safe elevator removed the ceiling on buildings — literally.

body.heading: The city grows upward
paragraphs: Once people trusted lifts, height became valuable instead of punishing: the top floor, once the cheapest for its stairs, became the penthouse. Elevators now move billions of passengers, and their safety record rests on descendants of Otis's spring — brakes that engage precisely when everything else fails.
The lesson is one inventors relearn in every field: often the breakthrough is not the machine, but the reason people finally trust it.

takeaway: Otis's safety brake, proved by cutting his own rope in 1854, made elevators trustworthy — and trustworthy elevators made skyscrapers possible.
